How Much Is $30 an Hour Annually? Full Pay & Budget Breakdown

Quick Answer

$30 an hour is $62,400 a year gross full-time — $1,200 a week and $5,200.00 a month before taxes.

Earning $30.00 an hour is one of the most significant compensation milestones in the American workforce. Crossing the thirty-dollar mark lifts you above the national median individual wage and places your gross earnings well into the sixties. Whether you are reviewing an offer letter for a skilled trade, an IT support position, a registered nursing role, or evaluating an hourly contract against a corporate salary, you need to know what that wage means in everyday dollars: How much is $30 an hour annually, what lands in your bank account after 2026 taxes, and what kind of lifestyle does it realistically support?

When engineering our calculation models at Hourly Wage Converter, one pattern stands out consistently: job seekers often look at $30 an hour and assume their take-home pay is a simple matter of multiplying by 40 hours. In practice, annual earnings fluctuate based on paid versus unpaid leave, overtime opportunities, payroll cycles, and state tax brackets. A $30-an-hour worker in Texas takes home a noticeably different paycheck than someone earning the exact same rate in California or New York.

In this guide, we break down the exact mathematics of $30 an hour across every payroll period, evaluate how unpaid time off and overtime alter your bottom line, map out 2026 federal and state tax withholdings, and walk through a realistic, balanced 50/30/20 monthly budget.

Calculate $30 an Hour Pay

$30 an Hour at a Glance: The Quick Answer

Assuming a standard full-time schedule of 40 hours per week across all 52 weeks of the year (2,080 annual working hours), $30 an hour equals $62,400.00 per year in gross compensation before taxes and voluntary benefit deductions.

Here is how that $62,400 annual salary breaks down across every common payroll frequency:

Where Does $30 an Hour Put You in the US Economy?

According to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) and the U.S. Census Bureau, the national median personal income for full-time American workers hovers between $48,000 and $50,000 per year. Earning $62,400 annually places you comfortably above the national median, landing in roughly the 55th to 60th percentile of individual earners nationwide.

However, the purchasing power of $30 an hour varies considerably depending on geographic location:

  • Low-to-Mid Cost of Living Areas (e.g., Ohio, Indiana, Missouri, North Carolina): An annual gross of $62,400 affords a comfortable lifestyle. A single earner can rent a modern one- or two-bedroom apartment, maintain a reliable vehicle, save 15% to 20% toward retirement, and have ample room for discretionary spending.
  • High Cost of Living Metros (e.g., Seattle, New York City, Boston, San Francisco): Housing costs absorb a significantly higher share of net income. In these cities, $30 an hour often requires sharing living spaces with roommates or budgeting with disciplined precision to prevent cash flow strain.

The Exact Math: How $30 an Hour Converts Across Every Pay Period

Human Resources and payroll departments in North America rely on standard mathematical divisors to translate an hourly rate into periodic pay stubs. Here is the exact calculation progression for a $30 hourly wage at 40 hours per week across 52 paid weeks:

Annual Salary = Hourly Rate × Weekly Hours × Paid Weeks

Calculation: $30.00 × 40 hours × 52 weeks = $62,400.00 gross annual pay

Pay Period Calculation Formula Gross Amount Payroll Frequency Notes
Hourly Rate Base wage $30.00 Standard straight-time rate
Daily (8 Hours) $30.00 × 8 hours $240.00 Standard 8-hour workday
Weekly $30.00 × 40 hours $1,200.00 52 pay periods per calendar year
Biweekly $30.00 × 80 hours (or $62,400 ÷ 26) $2,400.00 Paid every two weeks (26 checks/year)
Semi-Monthly $62,400.00 ÷ 24 $2,600.00 Paid twice per month (24 checks/year)
Monthly Average $62,400.00 ÷ 12 $5,200.00 Derived from annual (not weekly × 4)
Quarterly $62,400.00 ÷ 4 $15,600.00 4 quarters per calendar year
Annual Total $30.00 × 2,080 hours $62,400.00 Standard full-time annual benchmark

For a detailed breakdown of how this wage compares to nearby wage tiers, check our guide on $30 an hour is how much a year. One tier down, $23 an hour comes to $47,840 a year — right at the national median.

How Unpaid Time Off Changes Your Annual Earnings

The standard $62,400 figure assumes that all 52 weeks of the calendar year are compensated. If your job offers comprehensive Paid Time Off (PTO), paid federal holidays, and paid sick leave, your gross salary remains $62,400 because paid days off are compensated at your regular straight-time rate.

However, if you work as a contractor, temporary professional, or work for an employer that does not offer paid leave, taking time away from work directly reduces your income. For every week you take off without pay, you lose 40 hours of billable wages ($1,200 gross).

52 Paid Weeks (Full PTO)

If you take four unpaid weeks off each year (e.g., unpaid summer vacation and company winter shutdown), your paid weeks drop to 48 (1,920 hours), resulting in $57,600.00 gross. When evaluating job offers that lack PTO, always deduct planned unpaid time to see the real income you will receive.

Overtime Math: Pushing $30/Hour Above $74,000

Under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA), eligible non-exempt employees who work more than 40 hours in a single workweek are entitled to overtime pay at a minimum rate of 1.5 times their regular hourly rate (time-and-a-half).

Overtime Hourly Rate = Base Wage × 1.5 = $30.00 × 1.5 = $45.00 / hour

Every hour worked over 40 adds $45.00 straight to your gross paycheck.

Because your overtime rate is $45.00 an hour, even modest extra hours each week create a dramatic boost in total annual earnings. Consider what happens when you work 5 overtime hours each week (45 total weekly hours):

  • Base Regular Pay (40 hours): 40 × $30.00 = $1,200.00 / week ($62,400.00 / year)
  • Overtime Pay (5 hours): 5 × $45.00 = $225.00 / week ($11,700.00 / year)
  • Total Weekly Gross Compensation: $1,200.00 + $225.00 = $1,425.00 / week
  • Total Annual Gross Income: $1,425.00 × 52 weeks = $74,100.00 / year

Working just 5 hours of overtime per week increases your annual income by $11,700.00, transforming a $62,400 salary into $74,100. If your company or union contract pays double time (2.0× or $60.00/hour) for holiday or Sunday shifts, earnings accelerate even faster. How Much Is $30 an Hour After 2026 Taxes? (Take-Home Breakdown)

Gross compensation is what you earn; net take-home pay is what deposits into your checking account. To calculate your real take-home pay on a $62,400 annual salary, we must apply 2026 federal income tax brackets, mandatory FICA payroll contributions, and state tax variations for a single filer taking the standard deduction.

1. Mandatory Federal Payroll Withholdings (2026 Tax Year)

  • Gross Annual Income: $62,400.00
  • 2026 Standard Deduction (Single Filer): $16,100.00
  • Taxable Income: $62,400.00 − $16,100.00 = $46,300.00
  • Federal Income Tax Breakdown:
    • 10% on the first $12,400.00 = $1,240.00
    • 12% on the remaining $33,900.00 ($46,300 − $12,400) = $4,068.00
    • Total 2026 Federal Income Tax: $1,240.00 + $4,068.00 = $5,308.00 (Effective federal tax rate ~8.51%)
  • FICA Taxes (Mandatory Federal Contributions):
    • Social Security (6.2% on total gross): $62,400.00 × 6.2% = $3,868.80
    • Medicare (1.45% on total gross): $62,400.00 × 1.45% = $904.80
    • Total FICA Taxes (7.65%): $4,773.60
  • Total Federal Withholdings (Income Tax + FICA): $5,308.00 + $4,773.60 = $10,081.60

2. State Income Tax Impact & Net Take-Home Pay

State taxes create the largest divergence in your actual paycheck. Here is how your take-home pay looks across three typical state tax environments:

State Tax Tier Representative States Annual Net Pay Monthly Net Biweekly Net Check
No State Income Tax (0%) Texas, Florida, Washington, Tennessee, Nevada, Wyoming, Alaska, South Dakota ~$52,318.40 ~$4,360.00 ~$2,012.00
Moderate State Tax (~4.5%) Illinois, Pennsylvania, North Carolina, Arizona, Indiana, Michigan ~$49,510.00 ~$4,126.00 ~$1,904.00
Higher State Tax (~6%–8%) California, New York, New Jersey, Oregon, Minnesota, Massachusetts ~$48,518.00 ~$4,043.00 ~$1,866.00

Estimates reflect 2026 federal brackets, standard deduction, and FICA for a single filer with no dependents. Voluntary deductions (such as health insurance premiums or traditional 401(k) contributions) will reduce taxable income and net pay further. A Realistic 50/30/20 Monthly Budget on $30 an Hour

With an average net take-home pay of $4,126.00 to $4,360.00 per month (depending on your state), you have a solid foundation for disciplined financial management. Applying the popular 50/30/20 budget framework creates a sustainable balance between living expenses, discretionary enjoyment, and long-term wealth building.

50% Needs
~$2,063 – $2,180 / mo

• Housing/Rent: ~$1,250 – $1,300 (Follows the standard 25%–30% rule of gross $5,200)
• Utilities & Internet: ~$220
• Groceries & Household: ~$350
• Transportation & Insurance: ~$280

30% Wants
~$1,238 – $1,308 / mo

• Dining Out & Socializing: ~$400
• Entertainment & Streaming: ~$120
• Gym, Wellness & Hobbies: ~$150
• Travel & Discretionary Shopping: ~$570

20% Savings & Debt
~$825 – $872 / mo

• Emergency Fund: ~$300 (Aim for 3–6 months of essential living expenses)
• Roth IRA / 401(k) Match: ~$400 ($4,800/year invested compound growth)
• Extra Debt Paydown: ~$125 – $172

The 30% Housing Rule at $30/Hour: Financial planners generally recommend keeping total housing costs (rent or mortgage plus home insurance and property taxes) under 30% of your gross monthly income. On a gross salary of $5,200.00 per month, your recommended maximum housing cost is $1,560.00 per month ($5,200 × 30%). Keeping rent closer to $1,250 to $1,300 provides a comfortable buffer for unexpected expenses and faster wealth building.

Comparing a $30 Hourly Rate to Salaried Job Offers

When transitioning between jobs, workers frequently compare a $30/hour position against an exempt salaried offer of $60,000, $65,000, or $70,000. It is easy to look at a $65,000 salary offer and assume it is superior to a $30/hour position ($62,400). However, the critical variable is uncompensated overtime.

Hourly Position

Offer A: $30.00 / Hour

  • Guaranteed straight-time pay for every hour clocked
  • 1.5× Overtime ($45.00/hr) beyond 40 hours
  • Strong legal separation of personal time
  • Unpaid holiday closures reduce pay if no PTO
40 hrs/wk = $62,400.00 gross | 45 hrs/wk = $74,100.00 gross!
Salaried Position

Offer B: $65,000 Salaried

  • Predictable, consistent paycheck every month
  • Paid federal holidays and PTO included
  • Overtime-exempt; evening work is uncompensated
  • 45-hour workweek drops effective pay to $27.78/hr!
$65,000 ÷ 2,340 hours (45 hrs/wk) = $27.78 / hour effective

As illustrated above, if the $65,000 salaried role routinely demands 45 hours per week of meetings, emails, and evening responsibilities, your effective hourly rate drops to $27.78 per hour. Meanwhile, an hourly worker logging those same 45 hours earns $74,100.00 per year thanks to overtime pay. Common Paycheck Math Mistakes to Avoid

When converting $30 an hour into annual, monthly, or paycheck figures, watch out for these frequent calculation traps:

Mistake 1: Multiplying weekly pay by 4 to get monthly pay ($4,800 vs. $5,200).

Multiplying your $1,200 weekly pay by 4 yields $4,800.00, which undercounts your true monthly earnings by $400 every single month! There are 52 weeks in a year, meaning the average month contains 4.333 weeks (52 ÷ 12). Your true average monthly gross is $5,200.00 ($62,400 ÷ 12).

Mistake 2: Confusing biweekly (26 checks) with semi-monthly (24 checks).

Biweekly employees are paid every two weeks (26 pay periods per year), resulting in gross checks of $2,400.00. Semi-monthly employees are paid twice a month (e.g., on the 15th and last day, 24 checks per year), resulting in gross checks of $2,600.00. While annual pay is identical ($62,400), each individual check differs by $200.00.

Mistake 3: Forgetting mandatory FICA taxes (7.65%).

Many online salary discussions focus entirely on federal income tax brackets and completely forget FICA contributions. Social Security (6.2%) and Medicare (1.45%) deduct $4,773.60 from your gross salary before you pay a single dollar of income tax.

Mistake 4: Budgeting rent or fixed loan payments on gross pay.

Never budget living expenses using your $5,200 gross income. Base your lease agreements, car notes, and recurring obligations on your actual take-home cash flow ($4,043 to $4,360/month depending on state taxes and benefit deductions).

Mistake 5: Treating occasional overtime as guaranteed base salary.

Overtime can be eliminated by company management during budget cuts or economic slowdowns. Build your essential lifestyle around your base 40-hour take-home pay and channel overtime windfalls directly into emergency reserves, debt reduction, or investments.

Frequently Asked Questions About $30 an Hour Annually

Here are clear, direct answers to common questions about earning $30 an hour:

How much is $30 an hour annually?

At a standard full-time schedule of 40 hours per week for 52 paid weeks (2,080 working hours), $30 an hour equals an estimated gross annual salary of $62,400 before taxes and deductions. If you take 2 weeks of unpaid vacation (50 paid weeks), your gross annual pay drops to $60,000.

How much is $30 an hour per month?

At 40 hours per week, $30 an hour averages $5,200.00 per month before taxes ($62,400 divided by 12 months). A common calculation mistake is multiplying weekly pay ($1,200) by 4 to get $4,800, which undercounts your true monthly earnings by $400 because a calendar month averages 4.33 weeks.

How much is $30 an hour on a biweekly paycheck?

On a standard biweekly pay schedule (every two weeks, 26 pay periods per year), earning $30 an hour yields a gross paycheck of $2,400.00 for 80 regular hours worked ($30 × 80). After 2026 federal income tax and FICA withholdings (7.65%), a single filer with no state income tax takes home approximately $2,012 per paycheck.

How much is $30 an hour after taxes?

For a single filer taking the 2026 standard deduction ($16,100), federal income tax is $5,308.00 and FICA taxes (Social Security and Medicare) total $4,773.60. In states with no income tax (such as Texas or Florida), annual take-home pay is approximately $52,318.40 (~$4,360/month). In states with moderate income taxes (~4.5%), take-home pay is approximately $49,510 (~$4,126/month). In higher-tax states, net pay is roughly $48,518 (~$4,043/month).

Is $30 an hour considered a good wage?

Yes, $30 an hour ($62,400 gross per year) is well above the median individual income in the United States (around $48,000–$50,000). It allows a single earner to live comfortably in most low-to-moderate cost-of-living areas, cover independent housing following the 30% rent rule (up to $1,300/month), and consistently save for retirement and emergencies.

What is time-and-a-half overtime for $30 an hour?

Under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA), time-and-a-half overtime is 1.5 times your base wage. For $30 an hour, your overtime rate is $45.00 per hour ($30 × 1.5). Working just 5 hours of overtime per week adds $225.00 in weekly pay ($11,700 over 52 weeks), boosting your total gross income to $74,100.00 per year.

Key Takeaways & Next Steps

Summary Checklist for $30/Hour Earners

  • Annual Gross Baseline: $30 an hour equals $62,400.00 per year based on 2,080 full-time hours (40 hours/week across 52 weeks).
  • Average Monthly Earnings: Monthly gross pay is $5,200.00. Remember that a calendar month has 4.33 weeks, not 4.
  • 2026 Net Take-Home Pay: After federal income tax ($5,308) and FICA ($4,773.60), net take-home pay ranges from ~$48,518 to ~$52,318 annually (~$4,043 to ~$4,360/month), depending on state income tax.
  • Overtime Power: Overtime is paid at $45.00/hour. Working 5 extra hours per week adds $11,700 annually, pushing gross income to $74,100.
  • Prudent Housing Target: Following the 30% rule of gross income, keep monthly rent or mortgage payments at or below $1,300 to $1,560.

  1. Full-time gross pay is $62,400 a year, or $5,200.00 a month before taxes.
  2. Weekly pay × 4 understates a month — $1,200 a week × 4 gives $4,800, which is $400 a month short.
  3. Gross is the starting point, not the paycheck — 2026 federal and FICA taxes and a realistic take-home budget are covered inside.
